title: Redox reactions
subject: Chemistry
summary: Redox reactions involve simultaneous oxidation (loss of electrons) and reduction (gain of electrons).
points: Oxidation number is a bookkeeping number that tracks electron loss and gain in a compound.
The oxidising agent is reduced and the reducing agent is oxidised.
Redox reactions balance by the oxidation-number method or the half-reaction (ion–electron) method.
Disproportionation is a reaction where one element is both oxidised and reduced.

formulas.name: Oxidation
formulas.expr: loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number

formulas.name: Reduction
formulas.expr: gain of electrons, decrease in oxidation number

example: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is oxidised and copper ions are reduced.
mistakes: Assuming oxygen must be present for oxidation.
Forgetting that an oxidising agent is itself reduced.

title: States of matter and gas laws
subject: Chemistry
summary: Gases are described by the gas laws, and deviations from ideal behaviour reveal intermolecular attraction and molecular volume.
points: Boyle's law: at constant temperature PV is constant; Charles's law: V/T is constant at constant pressure.
The ideal gas equation PV = nRT combines the simple gas laws.
Dalton's law of partial pressures adds the contributions of each gas in a mixture.
Van der Waals equation corrects for molecular volume (b) and attraction (a).
Critical temperature is the highest temperature at which a gas can be liquefied by pressure alone.
example: At STP one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L.
mistakes: Using Celsius in gas-law calculations.
Expecting real gases to obey PV = nRT at high pressure.

title: Hydrogen and its compounds
subject: Chemistry
summary: Hydrogen is the lightest element and forms three isotopes; it shows both hydride-forming and unique bonding behaviour.
points: The isotopes are protium, deuterium and tritium, differing only in neutron number.
Hydrogen forms ionic hydrides with alkali metals, covalent hydrides with non-metals and interstitial hydrides with transition metals.
Hydrogen peroxide acts as both oxidising and reducing agent; its strength is expressed in volume or percentage.
Heavy water (D₂O) is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors.
example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O releases a large amount of energy, which is why hydrogen is studied as a fuel.
mistakes: Treating hydrogen as a halogen-like element in all reactions.
Forgetting that H₂O₂ can act as a reducing agent.

title: The s-block elements
subject: Chemistry
summary: Group 1 (alkali metals) and group 2 (alkaline earth metals) have outer ns¹ and ns² configurations and are highly reactive.
points: Alkali metals are soft, low density, and react vigorously with water to give hydroxides and hydrogen.
Reactivity increases down group 1 and down group 2 because ionisation energy falls.
Group 2 metals are harder and less reactive than group 1 and form mainly ionic compounds.
Compounds of group 1 and 2 are important industrially: sodium carbonate, plaster of Paris, lime, bleaching powder.
example: Sodium reacts with water giving sodium hydroxide and hydrogen, and the heat released can ignite the hydrogen.
mistakes: Expecting beryllium to behave like other group 2 metals.
Forgetting that group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group.

title: The p-block elements
subject: Chemistry
summary: The p-block covers groups 13 to 18, from boron and carbon families through the halogens to the noble gases.
points: p-block elements have outer configuration ns²np¹⁻⁶ and show a wide range of oxidation states.
Down a group, metallic character increases and the inert-pair effect appears for heavier elements.
Group 15 includes nitrogen and phosphorus; group 16 includes oxygen and sulphur; group 18 are noble gases.
Anomalies at the top of each group (boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine) come from their small size.
example: Phosphorus exists as white (P₄) and red allotropes; white phosphorus is far more reactive and is stored under water.
mistakes: Assuming all p-block elements are non-metals.
Ignoring the inert-pair effect for heavier elements.

title: Organic chemistry: basic principles
subject: Chemistry
summary: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds; structure, bonding and electronic effects explain their reactions.
points: Carbon shows tetravalency and catenation, which is why it forms chains, branches and rings.
Functional groups such as −OH, −CHO, −COOH and −NH₂ decide the chemical behaviour of a molecule.
Inductive, resonance and hyperconjugation effects explain stability and acidity.
Electrophiles accept electron pairs and nucleophiles donate them; reaction types are substitution, addition and elimination.

formulas.name: IUPAC order
formulas.expr: prefix + word root + primary suffix + secondary suffix

example: CH₃CH₂OH and CH₃OCH₃ are isomers with very different chemistry because their functional groups differ.
mistakes: Naming the longest chain incorrectly.
Confusing structural with stereoisomerism.

title: Hydrocarbons
subject: Chemistry
summary: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen and are classified as alkanes, alkenes, alkynes or aromatics.
points: Alkanes are saturated and react mainly by free-radical substitution.
Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated and undergo addition reactions; Markovnikov's rule predicts where hydrogen adds.
Benzene is aromatic: its delocalised six π electrons give extra stability and substitution rather than addition is preferred.
Ozonolysis and oxidation locate double bonds and distinguish unsaturated hydrocarbons.

formulas.name: Markovnikov
formulas.expr: H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens

example: Ethene + Br₂ in CCl₄ decolourises bromine water, a test for unsaturation.
mistakes: Expecting benzene to add bromine easily.
Forgetting Markovnikov's rule for unsymmetrical alkenes.

title: Environmental chemistry
subject: Chemistry
summary: Environmental chemistry studies how chemical substances move through air, water and soil and how they affect life.
points: Air pollution includes oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, carbon monoxide and particulates; some form acid rain.
Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons react in sunlight.
Water pollution is measured by dissolved oxygen, BOD and COD; excess nutrients cause eutrophication.
Green chemistry aims to design processes that use fewer hazardous substances and produce less waste.

formulas.name: BOD
formulas.expr: oxygen consumed by microbes per litre of water

example: Acid rain lowers soil pH and leaches aluminium, damaging roots and aquatic life.
mistakes: Confusing BOD with COD.
Thinking ozone in the troposphere is protective.

title: The solid state
subject: Chemistry
summary: Solids are crystalline or amorphous; the arrangement of particles decides their density, melting point and electrical behaviour.
points: Crystalline solids have long-range order and sharp melting points; amorphous solids do not.
Unit cells are primitive, body-centred or face-centred, with coordination numbers 6, 8 and 12.
Packing efficiency is 52% for simple cubic, 68% for body-centred and 74% for face-centred cubic.
Defects such as Schottky and Frenkel change density and sometimes conductivity.
Solids are classified as ionic, covalent, metallic or molecular on the basis of the forces holding them.
example: Sodium chloride has a face-centred cubic chloride lattice with sodium ions in octahedral holes.
mistakes: Forgetting Z, the number of atoms per unit cell.
Mixing up Schottky (missing pair) and Frenkel (displaced ion) defects.

title: Solutions and colligative properties
subject: Chemistry
summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture; its concentration can be expressed in several ways and its properties depend on solute amount.
points: Molarity changes with temperature because volume changes; molality and mole fraction do not.
Raoult's law states that the vapour pressure of a solvent falls in proportion to the solute's mole fraction.
Colligative properties — vapour pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure — depend on the number of particles, not their identity.
Van't Hoff factor accounts for association or dissociation of solute particles.

formulas.name: Molality
formulas.expr: m = moles of solute / kg of solvent

example: Adding salt lowers the freezing point of water, which is why it melts ice on roads.
mistakes: Using molarity in temperature-dependent formulas.
Ignoring the van't Hoff factor for electrolytes.

title: Surface chemistry
subject: Chemistry
summary: Surface chemistry studies phenomena at interfaces: adsorption, catalysis, colloids and emulsions.
points: Adsorption is the accumulation of molecules on a surface; physisorption is weak and reversible, chemisorption is strong and specific.
A catalyst speeds a reaction without being consumed and provides an alternative path with lower activation energy.
Colloids have particles between 1 nm and 1000 nm; they scatter light (Tyndall effect) and carry charge.
Coagulation, peptisation and dialysis are ways of handling colloidal systems.
example: Milk is an emulsion of fat in water, stabilised by protein emulsifiers.
mistakes: Confusing adsorption with absorption.
Assuming a catalyst changes the equilibrium position.

title: The d- and f-block elements
subject: Chemistry
summary: Transition metals have partially filled d orbitals, giving variable oxidation states, colour and catalytic activity.
points: Transition metals show variable oxidation states because 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy.
Colour arises from d–d transitions; ions with empty or full d subshells are usually colourless.
They form complex compounds and are good catalysts due to variable oxidation states and surface adsorption.
The lanthanoids show the lanthanoid contraction, which makes later elements smaller than expected.
Metallurgy of these metals involves concentration, roasting or calcination, reduction and refining.
example: Fe²⁺ is green and Fe³⁺ is yellow-brown because their d–d transitions absorb different wavelengths.
aliases: general principles and processes of isolation of elements
mistakes: Calling zinc a typical transition metal; its d subshell is full.
Ignoring the lanthanoid contraction when comparing radii.

title: Haloalkanes and haloarenes
subject: Chemistry
summary: Haloalkanes and haloarenes contain halogen atoms attached to sp³ and sp² carbons respectively and differ markedly in reactivity.
points: Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution by SN1 or SN2 pathways.
SN1 goes through a carbocation and is favoured by tertiary halides and polar protic solvents.
SN2 is a one-step backside attack favoured by primary halides and strong nucleophiles.
Haloarenes are much less reactive because of partial double-bond character and resonance stabilisation.
Elimination competes with substitution when a strong base is used.
example: Chlorobenzene resists hydrolysis while chloroethane reacts with aqueous alkali on heating.
mistakes: Assuming all halides react at the same rate.
Forgetting that SN1 racemises the product.

title: Alcohols, phenols and ethers
subject: Chemistry
summary: Alcohols have −OH on an sp³ carbon, phenols have −OH on a benzene ring, and ethers have an oxygen bridging two carbon groups.
points: Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary, which decides their oxidation products.
Phenol is more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised.
Alcohols react with sodium, undergo dehydration and esterification; phenols undergo electrophilic substitution readily.
Williamson synthesis makes ethers from an alkoxide and a primary alkyl halide.
example: Ethanol on oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ gives ethanal and then ethanoic acid.
mistakes: Thinking phenol is a typical alcohol.
Using a tertiary halide in Williamson synthesis; elimination dominates.

title: Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids
subject: Chemistry
summary: Aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group, and carboxylic acids combine a carbonyl with a hydroxyl group.
points: Aldehydes are oxidised easily; ketones resist oxidation, which distinguishes them.
Tollens' and Fehling's tests detect aldehydes through silver mirror or red precipitate formation.
Nucleophilic addition is the characteristic reaction of carbonyl compounds.
Carboxylic acids are acidic because the carboxylate ion is resonance-stabilised.
Aldol condensation and Cannizzaro reaction are important carbonyl reactions.

formulas.name: Tollens' reagent
formulas.expr: [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ reduces to Ag mirror with aldehydes

example: Propanal gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent; propanone does not.
mistakes: Expecting ketones to give Tollens' test.
Forgetting that formic acid also reduces Tollens' reagent.

title: Amines
subject: Chemistry
summary: Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
points: Amines are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary by the number of carbon groups on nitrogen.
Aliphatic amines are more basic than ammonia; aromatic amines are much less basic because the lone pair is delocalised.
Hofmann bromamide degradation converts an amide to a primary amine with one carbon less.
Amines react with nitrous acid differently depending on class, which is a useful test.
Diazonium salts are versatile intermediates for preparing substituted aromatic compounds.

formulas.name: Basicity order
formulas.expr: secondary aliphatic > primary > tertiary > NH₃ > aromatic amine

example: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because its lone pair participates in the ring's resonance.
mistakes: Assuming aromatic amines are stronger bases.
Confusing primary amine with primary alcohol.

title: Polymers
subject: Chemistry
summary: Polymers are large molecules built from repeating monomer units by addition or condensation polymerisation.
points: Addition polymerisation joins monomers with double bonds without losing any small molecule.
Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule such as water at each linkage.
Polymers may be linear, branched or cross-linked, which changes strength and flexibility.
Natural polymers include starch, cellulose, proteins and rubber; synthetic ones include polythene, PVC and nylon.

formulas.name: Degree of polymerisation
formulas.expr: number of monomer units in the chain

example: Bakelite is a thermosetting cross-linked polymer and cannot be remelted, unlike polythene.
mistakes: Calling all plastics thermoplastics.
Mixing up the monomers of nylon and polyester.

title: Chemistry in everyday life
subject: Chemistry
summary: Chemistry explains drugs, food additives, soaps and detergents, and the materials used in daily life.
points: Drugs act by affecting enzymes, receptors or cell membranes; antibiotics target bacteria specifically.
Soap is a sodium salt of a fatty acid and cleans by forming micelles around grease.
Detergents work in hard water because their calcium salts are soluble, unlike those of soap.
Artificial sweeteners, preservatives and antioxidants are food additives used in controlled amounts.

formulas.name: Soap
formulas.expr: RCOONa, with a long hydrocarbon tail

formulas.name: Micelle
formulas.expr: tails inward in grease, heads outward in water

example: Soap forms scum in hard water because calcium and magnesium salts of fatty acids are insoluble.
mistakes: Thinking detergents are biodegradable in all cases.
Assuming all drugs cure rather than manage symptoms.
